faq.a: Longshore drift is the movement of sand and pebbles along a coast. Waves carry sediment up the beach at an angle, it rolls straight back down, and each zigzag moves it sideways.
asks: How does sand move along a beach?

faq.a: Swash is the water rushing up the beach after a wave breaks. Backwash is the water draining back down the beach towards the sea.
Groynes are low walls built across a beach, out into the sea. They trap sand moved by longshore drift, keeping the beach from being washed away, but beaches further along can lose sand.
asks: Why are there wooden fences on beaches?

faq.a: A spit is a long ridge of sand or shingle that sticks out from the coast into the sea. It forms where longshore drift carries sand past a bend in the coastline.
Waves, storms and longshore drift are always moving sand, adding it in some places and removing it in others. Stormy winters often strip beaches; calm summers build them back.
asks: Why does a beach lose sand?

facts: Spurn Head in Yorkshire, England, is a sand spit about 5 kilometres long built by longshore drift.
Groynes trap sand on the up-drift side and can starve beaches further down the coast.
